posts.title: The cat could stay (birch pollen, not the cat)
posts.excerpt: How a sixty-minute history and skin-prick testing resolved severe spring symptoms while allowing an adult patient to keep their family cat.
posts.content:
A thirty-four-year-old adult patient arrived at our clinic at Linden Quay 14 on a Tuesday morning, exhausted by several months of relentless sneezing, itchy eyes, and waking up with a tight chest. The patient was convinced the cause was their two-year-old domestic cat. They had already arranged for a relative to temporarily take the cat, feeling an overwhelming sense of guilt and loss. Before taking such a permanent step, their general practitioner suggested booking a comprehensive sixty-minute first consultation with Dr Ines Marlow. Anonymised note: written with permission; details changed.

In allergy medicine, assumptions often develop when two events happen around the same period. The patient had adopted the cat during early spring of the previous year, shortly before symptoms initially appeared. Because the symptoms persisted into the autumn, the animal became the obvious focal point of blame. However, when Dr Ines Marlow took the full history during that initial hour, subtle inconsistencies emerged. The patient’s symptoms worsened dramatically whenever they walked along the canal paths of Ghent on breezy mornings, whereas petting the cat indoors rarely triggered sudden sneezing or skin hives.

To move beyond assumptions, nurse lead Leah Fontaine conducted a skin-prick test panel of twenty common allergens. Tiny droplets of purified extracts—including tree pollens, grass pollens, house dust mites, and cat dander—were placed in a neat grid along the patient's forearm, followed by gentle surface lancet pricks. After fifteen quiet minutes by our curtained consulting room window, the skin reactions were carefully measured. The cat dander site showed no reaction whatsoever, completely flat and pale. In contrast, the birch pollen extract produced a clear, raised wheal measuring six millimetres, alongside a moderate reaction to alder pollen.

The clinical picture suddenly became clear. The patient was not allergic to their cat. Instead, they suffered from significant seasonal allergic rhinitis triggered primarily by birch and alder pollens. The reason their symptoms appeared to linger into late autumn was twofold: the patient was also mildly sensitised to indoor house dust mites, and the cat’s outdoor explorations through local vegetation had carried pollen residues indoors on its fur. The animal was acting as an unwitting vehicle for environmental pollen rather than being the source of an immune reaction.

Dr Ines Marlow and dietitian Noor Aziz formulated a written one-page avoidance plan that the patient could take home immediately. Rather than giving away a cherished pet, the plan outlined targeted pollen management. It recommended keeping bedroom windows closed during peak morning tree pollen releases, wiping the cat’s coat with a damp microfibre cloth after it returned from outside, and vacuuming living areas with high-efficiency filtration. Dr Marlow also initiated a course of targeted nasal spray and non-sedating antihistamines to stabilise the mucosal barrier.

A follow-up review was booked for twelve weeks later. When the patient returned to our Linden Quay rooms, the difference was remarkable. By implementing the simple environmental adjustments and managing pollen exposure proactively, their nasal congestion and ocular itching had resolved. Most importantly, the cat could stay. As the patient noted on their fridge-bound plan, understanding the exact trigger restored calm to their home without unnecessary sacrifice.

What we did

A sixty-minute history, a skin-prick panel read after fifteen minutes, a one-page plan and a review at twelve weeks.

posts.title: A rash after every run
posts.excerpt: A runner kept getting hives after morning runs. The history, not the track, held the answer.
posts.content:
A man in his forties ran every morning before work and came out in hives on his arms about twenty minutes after most runs. He had changed shoes, shirts and routes without any difference.

We spent most of the first hour on breakfast. The rash only came when he had eaten wheat-based cereal before running, and never on rest days with the same cereal. That pattern, a food that is tolerated at rest and reacts with exercise, is one we ask about early.

Testing and a careful food history agreed with the pattern. The written plan changed one thing, the order of breakfast and training, and kept every other food he liked. He still runs at seven.

What we did: a history, a skin-prick panel (€90), a one-page plan with a simple rule for training days, and a follow-up review (€80) at 12 weeks.

Case notes are anonymised and written with permission; details changed.

posts.title: Peanut, at four, one spoon at a time
posts.excerpt: A four-year-old came to the Wednesday children’s clinic for a supervised oral food challenge, one measured spoon at a time.
posts.content:
A four-year-old had avoided peanut since a mild reaction at two. His parents were tired of reading labels and unsure whether the allergy was still there.

At the Wednesday children’s clinic Dr Weber and our nurse set up a supervised oral food challenge, a half-day visit (€260) with a small table, a box of building blocks and a series of tiny, timed doses. Between each dose the boy built a tower with his father while we watched his skin and breathing.

The challenge told us what we were dealing with and what we were not. The family left with a written plan for home and school, and a review at twelve weeks to decide the next step.

What we did: a supervised oral food challenge (€260), a written plan for home and school, and a review at 12 weeks.

Case notes are anonymised and written with permission; details changed.

posts.title: The watch strap (nickel, patch test)
posts.excerpt: Itchy red skin under a watch strap for two years. A three-visit patch test series found nickel.
posts.content:
A woman in her fifties had a ring of red, itchy skin under her wristwatch for two years. Creams helped for a week and the rash returned every time she wore the watch.

Contact allergy does not show on a skin-prick test, so we booked a patch test series: three visits in one week (€210), with small test squares on the upper back that stay in place between visits. Leah read them on day two and day four.

Nickel gave a clear reaction. The plan listed the places nickel hides, from buckles to coins, and what to choose instead, so the list now lives in her wallet. A steel-free strap solved the watch.

What we did: a patch test series over three visits (€210), a written list of nickel sources, and a review at 12 weeks.

Case notes are anonymised and written with permission; details changed.

posts.title: Lung function on Saturdays
posts.excerpt: Saturday mornings are for testing only: spirometry, FeNO and skin-prick panels, with no consultations.
posts.content:
Our Saturday clinic runs from 9:00 to 12:30 and is for testing only. There are no first consultations, so the rooms stay quiet and the tests can take the time they need.

Samir Haddad, our respiratory physiologist, runs lung function and FeNO (30 minutes, €75): you breathe out into a small device, rest, and try again. The result gives us a number for airway inflammation that a history alone cannot give.

Skin-prick panels (40 minutes, €90) also run on Saturdays. If you work in the week, tell Grace when you book and she will fit the test around the history visit.

What we do: lung function and FeNO (€75) and skin-prick panels (€90) on Saturday mornings.
